syllabusTopics: Gaseous state: Kinetic theory of gas and its postulates
Gas laws: Boyle's law, Charles' law, Avogadro's law, combined gas equation, Dalton's law of partial pressure, Graham's law of diffusion
Ideal gas and ideal gas equation; universal gas constant and its significance
Deviation of real gas from ideality (solving related numerical problems based on gas laws)
Liquid state: physical properties of liquids — evaporation and condensation, vapour pressure and boiling point, surface tension and viscosity (qualitative idea only)
Solid state: types of solids, amorphous and crystalline solids
Efflorescent, deliquescent and hygroscopic solids; crystallization and crystal growth; water of crystallization
Introduction to unit crystal lattice and unit cell

card.title: Deviation of Real Gases from Ideality

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Real gases break the kinetic theory's two idealisations, and van der Waals priced each break: molecular **volume** shrinks the free space to (V − nb), and intermolecular **attraction** softens wall impacts, adding a(n/V)² to the pressure — together, **(P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT**.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - (P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT - Per mole: (P + a/V²)(V − b) = RT - Z = PV/nRT (Z = 1 ideal) - Boyle temperature: Z ≈ 1 over wide P range

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **b is roughly four times the actual molecular volume, not equal to it:** the excluded sphere around each molecule doubles its radius — a detail examiners like to probe.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "A real gas deviates most from ideal behaviour at high pressure and low temperature, where molecular volume and intermolecular attraction can no longer be neglected."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The CO₂ fire extinguisher*** — CO₂ liquefies at ~60 atm room temperature (a = 3.59): attraction plus pressure does what cooling does for nitrogen.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: deviation of real gas from ideality, solving related numerical problems based on gas laws (within States of Matter).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Deviation dial: "high P pushes Z up, low T pulls Z down". a ladder: H₂O > NH₃ > CO₂ > O₂ > H₂ > He. b ≈ 4 × molecular volume. Ideal zone: hot and dilute.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Van der Waals' two corrections are the kinetic theory's failed postulates 1 and 3 made quantitative — the equation is the ideal law plus honest accounting.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Real gases: finite molecular volume + intermolecular attraction. Van der Waals: (P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT; a = attraction (large for NH₃ 4.17, CO₂ 3.59, H₂O 5.46; tiny for He 0.034, H₂ 0.244); b = volume ≈ 4× molecular volume. Max deviation: high P (Z > 1, volume term) and low T (Z < 1, attraction term).…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Helium's near-zero a is why it stays liquid only at 4 K and why it escapes Earth's gravity — the least sticky, most elusive gas in the atmosphere.

rows.text: **NEB-style (2m): Ammonia liquefies under pressure at room temperature but nitrogen does not. rows.text: Compare the a and b values of CO₂ and H₂ and predict which liquefies more easily.  ·  State the limit / condition where a formula or rule stops being valid before applying it.  ·  Limit to remember: ideal gas equation pv = nrt; from kinetic theory p = ⅓ (nm/m)⟨c²⟩, so pv = ⅓n m⟨c²⟩.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ## 6. Common Confusions **Deviation has two directions:** high pressure inflates volume (Z > 1) while low temperature deflates pressure (Z < 1) — "deviates" does not mean one sign.  ·  **a and b are gas-specific constants, not universal:** R is universal; a and b must be looked up per gas — quoting R's value for a is a mark-losing slip.  ·  **Liquefaction needs attraction, not just pressure:** a large a means the gas can be liquefied near room temperature; a tiny a (He) demands extreme cooling first.
